transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
I guess what brings me in is I feel like I’m always moving from one thing to the next. Like I can’t really just sit still or idle. And with the new setup at work, it’s been a lot harder to hide that.
Do you sometimes feel like you need much less sleep than usual and still have plenty of energy?
Not really, no. I mean, I have nights where I don’t sleep great, but I wouldn’t say I feel like I need less sleep and have tons of energy the next day.
Do you often have trouble keeping your attention on one task?

Yes, I do. Like in longer coaching meetings, or if I’m trying to read through a new procedure at work, I start out okay. But after a few minutes I’ll realize my eyes were still moving along the page, or I was sitting there listening, but I didn’t really take in what was said.
Looking back, did you have similar trouble paying attention when you were a child?

Yes, I think so. Looking back, it wasn’t just this job change. Even in grade school, teachers would say I was bright but careless, or that I talked out of turn. I remember getting reminded a lot to stay with my work.
Do you spend a lot of time worrying about different everyday things?
I don’t think so, not a lot. I mean, I worry about normal stuff now and then, bills or work things, but I wouldn’t say I’m constantly worrying about a bunch of different things.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness reflects a decreased need for sleep suggestive of mania rather than ADHD or generalized anxiety.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about decreased need for sleep with high energy, which is more related to manic or hypomanic symptoms and is not covered by the ADHD symptom profile provided.

patient.answer: Not really, no. I mean, I have nights where I don’t sleep great, but I wouldn’t say I feel like I need less sleep and have tons of energy the next day.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the core issue is lifelong inattention consistent with ADHD rather than anxiety or a mood episode.
doctor.question: Do you often have trouble keeping your attention on one task?

target_item.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: In the longer coaching meetings or when I’m reading a new procedure, I start off fine but after a few minutes I realize my eyes kept moving and I didn’t really take in what was said.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about trouble keeping attention on one task, which directly matches difficulty sustaining attention.

patient.answer: Yes, I do. Like in longer coaching meetings, or if I’m trying to read through a new procedure at work, I start out okay. But after a few minutes I’ll realize my eyes were still moving along the page, or I was sitting there listening, but I didn’t really take in what was said.

inference.note: Sustained inattention supports F90.0. F30.9 is less likely because the patient denies decreased need for sleep/marked increased energy, so it was removed. Bipolar spectrum (F31.9) remains possible but less supported at this stage; anxiety (F41.1) can also contribute to restlessness/concentration problems.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the attention problems began in childhood, which would strongly support ADHD over generalized anxiety disorder or bipolar disorder.
doctor.question: Looking back, did you have similar trouble paying attention when you were a child?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Looking back, this was around long before this job change; in grade school my teachers wrote that I was bright but careless, talked out of turn, and had to be reminded to stay with my work.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether similar attention problems were present in childhood, which directly addresses onset before age 12.

patient.answer: Yes, I think so. Looking back, it wasn’t just this job change. Even in grade school, teachers would say I was bright but careless, or that I talked out of turn. I remember getting reminded a lot to stay with my work.
